title: Betsy and the Moonlight Path
markdown:
Betsy the beaver loved her home by Whispering Creek. A happy familiar place, always filled with the comforting smell of damp earth and the gentle musical gurgle of the water. She spent her days as busy as a bee, patting mud into place and carefully adding sturdy twigs to her ever-growing dam. Her lodge was the coziest place in the entire woods, wonderfully warm and perfectly dry, always smelling faintly of fresh pine needles. She felt completely safe nestled amongst the reeds and rustling trees. She knew every tiny ripple, every secret rustle in the tall grass, every shadow that danced on the water. Her happy familiar world.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, painting the sky orange and purple, Betsy decided her lodge needed something extra special.

“Moon-moss.” Whiskers twitching with a grand idea. “That’s exactly what will make my lodge extra extra cozy for the moonbeams.”

She knew the most beautiful moon-moss, the kind that practically glowed, only grew on the far side of Whispering Creek, where the shadows grew long and very deep. She would have to cross the water. As she thought about it, a little shiver ran right down her furry spine. The creek looked so dark and seemed so very wide when the sun said goodnight. Paws a little clammy. Tail a nervous little flick. She did not name the feeling. She only looked at the dark water and felt her dam-building courage go thin.

She took a deep breath and puffed out her chest. “I can build a bridge. A special night bridge.” Voice wobbled just a tiny bit. Her plan was to gather the sturdiest strongest branches and weave them all together. The moon, a slender sliver of silver, was just beginning to peek from behind gathering dark clouds. She would have to venture into the parts of the creek she usually avoided when the sun tucked itself away. The thought of the dark unknown water made her tummy do a funny little flip-flop. If she did not gather the moon-moss soon, the rare fireflies that only visited during the fullest moon would also leave, and she loved watching their twinkling dance.

With a determined wiggle of her nose she waded into the cool water at the edge. Soft squishy mud felt funny between her toes. She tried to carry a long heavy branch toward the middle, but it was just too slippery and fell with a loud splash. She flinched, ears perking. The sound seemed so incredibly loud in the hushed night. She could only see vague shapes in the dim moonlight. Every shadow seemed to twist and stretch, looking like a wobbly wiggly monster. She tried to push a big fallen log into place, but it bobbed and floated away, as if playing tag with the current. Suddenly a very loud ribbit echoed from the tall reeds. She froze completely still. Heart thumped like a tiny frantic drum. This is too scary. I should just go back. She almost turned around, ready to give up, her brave beaver spirit feeling very small.

Just then a soft almost musical croak drifted from a large velvety lily pad. As the sound left the pad, a shimmering silver stone, glowing with a gentle light, popped into existence on the water’s surface. Betsy blinked, utterly amazed. Another gentle croak, another silver stone, and then another, forming a wobbly little path. Peeking out from behind a large leafy fern was a small round frog with the most amazing eyes she had ever seen. They seemed to hold tiny captured pieces of the moon itself.

“Hello,” whispered the frog, voice as delicate as tiny bells. “I’m Oona. I can make stepping-stones, if you like. They’re made of moonlight and wishes.”

Betsy’s eyes widened. The perfect answer to her bridge problem, and something even more wonderful. A friend who could make actual magic.

She tentatively hopped onto the first silver stone. Surprisingly cool and wonderfully smooth beneath her paws. Oona gave another happy croak, and more stones appeared, stretching all the way across the creek, a glittering pathway to the other side. Betsy reached the far bank and quickly gathered the soft gently glowing moon-moss, its light making her paws feel warm. As she turned to come back, she saw Oona sitting all alone on her lily pad. A little sad, shining eyes gazing out at the water. Betsy suddenly realised that while making stepping-stones was a wonderful trick, it was also a little bit lonely without anyone to share it with. She really wanted to share her cozy lodge, but if she took Oona with her, she would not have her special stones to get back. She would have to leave her half-built bridge behind, unfinished. She hesitated, paws still on the soft moss. She pictured her lodge, warm and dry, moonlight dappling through the reeds. Then her gaze fell upon Oona’s wide lonely eyes, which seemed to hold all the quiet sadness of the night. A flutter of warmth, like a tiny spark, ignited deep in her chest, brighter than any moonbeam. With a soft sigh she let go of the unfinished bridge, the sturdy branches now just twigs at the mercy of the creek, and turned fully toward her new friend.

“Oona, would you like to come to my lodge? I have plenty of room, and it’s very cozy inside. We can even share some berry tea.”

Oona’s big eyes lit up like tiny lanterns. A happy chirp, full of delight. Betsy stepped back onto the silver stones, and Oona croaked a shimmering path for them both. The stones gleamed, leading them over the dark deep water, not just to Betsy’s side, but all the way back toward the warmth and safety of the lodge. She did not need to finish her bridge tonight. She had Oona.

They sat together by the crackling fire, sipping sweet berry tea from little acorn cups. The soft glowing moon-moss made the whole place shimmer. Betsy no longer felt even a tiny shiver when she thought about the creek. She did not say giggles were the best bridge of all. She only poured Oona a second cup, listened to the creek gurgle past the unfinished twigs, and knew she could always ask for a path of shimmering light if she ever wanted the other side again.
